names.name: Paramātman (the supreme self, the soul fully manifest)

descriptions: the soul's own nature fully unveiled: infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy
who knows one knows all; who knows all knows one (Ācārāṅga 1.3.4)
formless being that perceives and knows, beyond comparison (Ācārāṅga 1.5.6)
abiding at the summit of the universe in unobstructed happiness (Aupapātika; Uttarādhyayana 36)
the pure, eternal law is non-harm, proclaimed by all Arhats (Ācārāṅga 1.4.1)
negations: not long or short, of no colour, smell, taste or touch; not female, male or neuter; beyond sound, reasoning and mind (Ācārāṅga 1.5.6)
not a creator or ruler of the world
not a single substance of which souls are parts
relation_to_self: Every soul is by nature what the Siddha is; bondage is karmic matter covering that nature, and liberation is its uncovering by one's own effort through the three jewels.
relation_to_world: The world is real, uncreated and eternal, made of souls and non-souls; the liberated know it entirely but neither make nor govern it.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.

names.name: kevala-jñāna (the knowledge in which the ultimate is realized)

descriptions: the infinite, supreme, unobstructed, complete and full knowledge and perception attained by Mahāvīra (Kalpa Sūtra)
the self is sāmāyika, and the self is the purpose of sāmāyika (Bhagavatī 1.9)
reachable in a female or male body, in any garb (Prajñāpanā 1; Uttarādhyayana 36)
relation_to_self: The self's own equanimous, knowing nature; the omniscient in his body continues to take food until nirvāṇa.
relation_to_world: As for the Jain tradition generally: real, uncreated, eternal.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.

names.name: the Jina (worshipped in his image, sthāpanā-jina)

descriptions: the liberated Jina, present to the worshipper through the consecrated image as a support for recalling his qualities
the model of the worshipper's own purified self
negations: the Jina does not receive offerings or grant favours
the image is not itself divine apart from what it represents
relation_to_self: Worship of the Jina's qualities purifies the worshipper toward the same state.
relation_to_world: Real and uncreated; the images and temples are supports within it.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance. Image worship here is devotion to the qualities of a liberated soul, not to a creator-god.

names.name: the Jina / Arihanta and the Siddhas

descriptions: the qualities of the Jina and the liberated soul, approached through the scripture, the mendicants and one's own equanimity, not through images
negations: not to be worshipped in images; worship that harms beings is not dharma
relation_to_self: The soul's own nature, realized by restraint and equanimity (sāmāyika).
relation_to_world: Real and uncreated; every being in it, down to the one-sensed, is to be protected.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.

descriptions: the soul freed from karma by restraint; only what stops karmic inflow belongs to the supramundane
negations: not reached by worldly merit or the preservation of bodily life
relation_to_self: The soul's own restraint and purity.
relation_to_world: Real and uncreated; worldly duty is distinct from spiritual dharma.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.

descriptions: from the standpoint of ultimate reality the self is unbound, untouched, not other, constant, undifferentiated and unconjoined (Samayasāra 14)
one, pure, made of perception and knowledge, formless; not an atom of anything else is mine (Samayasāra 38)
the knowing state beyond all stages of quality (Samayasāra 6)
free of the eighteen faults, including hunger and thirst (Niyamasāra 6)
negations: in truth there is no knowledge, conduct or faith as separate attributes of the knower (Samayasāra 7)
not reached in a clothed or female body
relation_to_self: The pure self is the soul's own nature now, seen from the ultimate standpoint; the conventional standpoint describes the bound soul in order to lead it there.
relation_to_world: Real and uncreated; karmic matter and the soul occasion each other's changes without either becoming the other.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance. Kundakunda's language of the pure self is sometimes compared with Advaita; the Digambara tradition insists the pure self is each individual soul's own, not a universal Brahman.

descriptions: the same liberation as for all Jains, open to women and reached by the three jewels, which are not deficient in any human
negations: not closed to women or to those clothed by exception
relation_to_self: The soul's own nature, as in the Jain tradition generally.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance. Known only from a few surviving works.

names.name: Jiṉaṉ / Iṟaivaṉ (the Lord, as the Jina)

descriptions: the Arhat saluted at the opening of Tamil Jain works; release (vīṭu) won by virtue (aṟam) and renunciation (tuṟavu)
relation_to_self: Release is the soul's freedom from karma through virtue, austerity and renunciation.
relation_to_world: Wealth, youth and the body are impermanent; the world is real but not to be clung to.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.

names.name: the self's own pure nature (as the object of 'true worship')

descriptions: worship is inner: the self's own pure nature, taught in scripture, not an image
relation_to_self: The pure self is to be realized within.
relation_to_world: Real; outward rites are not the path.
caveat: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.

names.name: the Jina (in the image, worshipped with non-living offerings)

descriptions: the pure self known through both standpoints held in their places (Ṭoḍarmal)
relation_to_world: Real; worship must not harm beings.
